name: RNN-CNN Hybrid
analogy: Think of it as two analysts on one desk. The first scans each short stretch of the chart for local shapes, such as a sharp rejection candle or a tight squeeze. The second reads the first analyst's notes in time order, remembers what came earlier, and makes the call.

steps.title: Cut the history into short stretches
steps.description: The recent history is divided into a series of short stretches in time order. Each stretch holds a few bars of price, volume and indicator values laid out like a small picture.
steps.inExample: The last 60 five-minute MNQ bars are cut into 12 stretches of 5 bars, each with 8 feature columns.

steps.title: Scan each stretch for local shapes
steps.description: The convolutional part slides small filters across each stretch. Each filter responds to one local shape, such as a rising run, a wide-range bar on heavy volume, or a flat squeeze. The result is a short list of shape scores for that stretch.
steps.inExample: Each 5-bar stretch is reduced to 16 shape scores; the stretch just before the close scores high on falling bars with rising volume.

steps.title: Line the shape scores up in time
steps.description: The shape scores of every stretch are lined up in time order, producing a sequence of short summaries that replaces the raw bars. This sequence is the handover from the first analyst to the second.
steps.inExample: The 12 stretches give a sequence of 12 summaries, each with 16 numbers.

steps.title: Read the sequence with memory
steps.description: The recurrent part, a long short-term memory network, reads the summaries one after another and keeps a running memory, deciding at each step what to hold on to and what to forget. This captures how the shapes developed over time, such as a squeeze followed by a break.
steps.inExample: Memory keeps the early quiet squeeze and the recent selling run, and drops the unremarkable stretches between them.

steps.title: Turn the final memory into a call
steps.description: The memory after the last stretch passes through a small output layer that turns it into class probabilities, here the chance of up versus down over the chosen horizon.
steps.inExample: The output layer gives a 44 percent chance of up and 56 percent chance of down over the next 6 bars.

steps.title: Train both parts together
steps.description: Both parts are trained end to end on past examples with known outcomes. Errors flow back through the memory part into the shape-scanning part, so the filters learn the shapes that matter for the memory, not shapes chosen by hand.
steps.inExample: After training on 12 months of bars, a filter that began as random noise can settle on spotting wide-range reversal bars.

useFor.task: Direction calls from the recent bar sequence
useFor.example: Predicting whether MNQ's close 6 bars after a 5-minute bar will be above that bar's close, from the previous 60 bars of price, volume and indicators.

useFor.task: Recognising multi-bar patterns that unfold over time
useFor.example: Detecting a squeeze followed by a breakout attempt, where both the shape of the bars and their order matter.
Labelling each 60-bar ES window as trending, ranging or volatile for a strategy that switches behaviour.
Feeding open, high, low, close, volume and a handful of the 151 technical indicators as columns so the shape scanner sees them together.

avoidWhen: You have mostly tabular features and few rows; gradient boosting finds thresholds in such tables with far less data than this network needs.
You need an explanation of exactly why the call was made; the learned filters and memory are hard to read, and a tree-based model gives clearer reasons.

example.scenario: At the close of the 14:35 five-minute MNQ bar, the model reads the last 60 bars as 12 stretches of 5 bars and outputs the chance that the close 6 bars later is higher than this close.

input.summary: A block of the last 60 bars with 8 columns each, normalised using only past data; five summary values are shown.

fields.name: bars in the window
fields.meaning: Five hours of 5-minute bars, the history the model sees.

fields.name: close of the latest bar
fields.meaning: The price at which the 14:35 bar closed.

fields.name: average true range, 14 bars
fields.meaning: Typical high-to-low travel of a recent bar.

fields.name: volume against its 20-bar average, latest bar
fields.meaning: Heavy trading in the latest bar compared with the recent norm.

fields.name: return over the last 12 bars
fields.value: minus about two fifths of a percent
fields.meaning: How much price fell over the previous hour.

fields.name: relative strength index, 14 bars
fields.meaning: A momentum reading from 0 to 100; low values mean persistent selling.

output.summary: Probabilities for the two classes, plus the call they imply.

fields.name: probability the close is higher 6 bars later
fields.meaning: The model's chance that price will be above the current close in 30 minutes.

fields.name: probability the close is lower 6 bars later
fields.meaning: The remaining chance, so the two add to 100 percent.

fields.name: call
fields.meaning: The side the probability favours when the dividing line is 50 percent.

example.reading: A 56 percent lean toward down is modest. Whether it earns money depends on trading costs: one MNQ point is worth 2 US dollars, so a 6-bar move needs to beat commission and slippage on average. Check the lean on walk-forward folds with costs before trusting it.
